summary_html: Cases arising on **federal lands/facilities** or involving **Indian children** invoke federal/tribal jurisdictional rules (VICAA for federal facilities; **ICWA** for Indian children and tribal preference/jurisdiction).
authority_html:
- **VICAA (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — federal-facility reporting mandates  
- **ICWA (25 U.S.C. §§ 1901–1963)** — tribal jurisdiction, placement preferences, notice to tribes

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to S.M.M.D. and T.A.D.
key_cases.holding: A tribal-state agreement under 25 U.S.C. § 1919(a) may vest a Nevada district court with subject-matter jurisdiction over an Indian child custody proceeding even where § 1911(a) would otherwise place exclusive jurisdiction in the tribal court.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling Nevada authority on when a state court may hear an ICWA case and on the tribal-notice requirements that travel with it.
key_cases.quote: We therefore uphold the district court's jurisdiction over Raena's relinquishment of parental rights under 25 U.S.C. § 1919

key_cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Domicile under ICWA is a matter of uniform federal law, and children domiciled on the reservation fall within the tribal court's exclusive jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a) even where the parents voluntarily gave birth off-reservation.
key_cases.relevance: The foundational federal authority on when a state court has no jurisdiction at all over an Indian child.
key_cases.quote: Section 1911(a) establishes exclusive jurisdiction in the tribal courts for proceedings concerning an Indian child

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: ICWA is a valid exercise of Congress's Article I authority over Indian affairs, its placement and procedural requirements do not violate the anticommandeering doctrine, and the equal protection and nondelegation challenges failed for lack of standing (so the constitutionality of the placement preferences remains formally open).
key_cases.relevance: Confirms that ICWA and its Nevada analogue in NRS Chapter 125E remain fully binding on state courts and agencies.
key_cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Sections 1912(f) and 1912(d) of ICWA do not bar termination of the rights of a parent who never had custody of the Indian child, because there is no 'continued custody' to be broken up and no family to preserve through remedial efforts.
key_cases.relevance: Narrows which ICWA protections attach when the Indian parent never had physical or legal custody.
key_cases.quote: we hold that neither § 1912(f) nor § 1912(d) bars the termination of his parental rights

key_cases.case_name: Phillip A. C. v. Central Council of the Tlingit & Haida Tribes of Alaska
key_cases.holding: A tribal enrollment officer's affidavit may be used to establish that a child is an Indian child subject to ICWA, but the adoptive parent must be given an opportunity to rebut it; an Indian tribe has independent standing under 25 U.S.C. § 1914 to challenge a voluntary adoption, and a violation of § 1913(a)'s consent-certification requirement makes the adoption order voidable rather than void. Reversed and remanded so the adoptive parent could present rebuttal evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Nevada's published answer to two practical ICWA questions the statute does not settle — how Indian-child status is proved in a state court and who may raise ICWA — and it confirms that the tribe can intervene in a voluntary adoption on its own footing.
key_cases.quote: a Native American tribe has independent standing under the ICWA to challenge the voluntary adoption of a Native American child

mandatory_reporters: Designated professionals only (not universal) — NRS 432B.220(1) and (4); any other person may make a report but is not required to (NRS 432B.220(5))

A person providing services licensed or certified in this State pursuant to, without limitation, NRS chapters 450B, 630, 630A, 631, 632, 633, 634, 634A, 634B, 635, 636, 637, 637B, 639, 640, 640A, 640B, 640C, 640D, 640E, 641, 641A, 641B, 641C, 641D or 653, or practicing as an emergency medical technician, advanced emergency medical technician or paramedic in this State under the Recognition of Emergency Medical Services Personnel Licensure Interstate Compact ratified by NRS 450B.145 — NRS 432B.220(4)(a)

Any personnel of a medical facility licensed pursuant to NRS chapter 449 who are engaged in the admission, examination, care or treatment of persons, or an administrator, manager or other person in charge of such a medical facility upon notification of suspected abuse or neglect of a child by a member of the staff of the medical facility — NRS 432B.220(4)(b)
Members of the clergy, practitioners of Christian Science and religious healers, unless the knowledge was acquired from the offender during a confession — NRS 432B.220(4)(d)
Persons employed by a public or private school and persons who serve as volunteers at such a school — NRS 432B.220(4)(e)

Any person who maintains or is employed by a facility or establishment that provides care for children, a children's camp or any other public or private facility, institution or agency furnishing care to a child — NRS 432B.220(4)(f)
Persons licensed under NRS chapter 424 to conduct a foster home — NRS 432B.220(4)(g)
Officers and employees of a law enforcement agency and adult or juvenile probation officers — NRS 432B.220(4)(h)
Attorneys, except as otherwise provided in NRS 432B.225 — NRS 432B.220(4)(i)

Any person who maintains, is employed by or serves as a volunteer for an agency or service which advises persons regarding the abuse or neglect of a child and refers them for help — NRS 432B.220(4)(j)
Persons employed by or serving as volunteers for a youth shelter — NRS 432B.220(4)(k)
Any adult employed by an entity that provides organized activities for children, including a school district or public school — NRS 432B.220(4)(l)
Persons enrolled with Medicaid to provide doula services — NRS 432B.220(4)(m)
Certified prevention specialists, peer recovery support specialists and peer recovery support specialist supervisors — NRS 432B.220(4)(n)

Reports must be made to an agency which provides child welfare services or to a law enforcement agency as soon as reasonably practicable and not later than 24 hours after the reporter knows or has reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused or neglected — NRS 432B.220(1)

timeline_requirements.deadline: An investigation must be initiated immediately if the report indicates that there is a high risk of serious harm to the child, that the child has suffered a fatality, or that the child is living in a household in which another child has died, or the child is seriously injured or has visible signs of physical abuse (NRS 432B.260(2)); otherwise the agency which provides child welfare services must conduct an evaluation not later than 3 days after the report or notification was received to determine whether an investigation is warranted (NRS 432B.260(3)) and, if it is, must initiate the investigation not later than 3 days after the evaluation is completed (NRS 432B.260(4))
timeline_requirements.starts_from: A report concerning the possible abuse or neglect of a child is received by an agency which provides child welfare services or by a law enforcement agency, or the child welfare agency is notified by a law enforcement agency that it has received such a report (NRS 432B.260(2) and (3))
